title: Mutation between sibling calls
topic: Recursion: local state, side effects and call trees
explanation:
Each call has its own local n. The outer call prints 2 and changes its n to 1 before calling f(1). That child prints 1, calls a base case, prints 0, and calls another base case.

The outer call then prints its unchanged local 1 and calls f(0). The tokens are 2 1 B 0 B 1 B.

title: Two evaluation side effects
topic: Recursion: local state, side effects and call trees
explanation:
Java evaluates the left call first. The outer --n changes 2 to 1 and sends 1 to the child. The later n-- sends the current 1 before changing the parent to 0.

Both f(1) calls return 2 and make three entries each. Including the outer entry gives value 4 and seven invocations.

title: Persistent memo versus entry counter
topic: Recursion: local state, side effects and call trees
explanation:
The counter increases before the base-case and cache tests. The first f(5) call enters nine times, including calls that immediately use saved results. It returns 5 and stores that result.

The second f(5) still enters once, then returns the saved 5. The printed values are 5 5 10.

title: Indirect recursion depth
topic: Recursion: local state, side effects and call trees
explanation:
The calls are a(10), b(9), a(4), b(3), a(1), and b(0). The first five calls print their arguments. The last call increases calls, then returns without printing.

Therefore, the output is 10 9 4 3 1 | 6. Each pair of calls roughly halves a variable starting argument, giving logarithmic depth.

title: Accumulator still uses frames
topic: Recursion: local state, side effects and call trees

options.D: Θ(log n) time, Θ(log n) stack

explanation:
Each call reduces n by one and makes one further call. The chain contains n+1 entries through n=0. Each entry does constant arithmetic under the question's overflow assumption.

Time is Θ(n). Java does not guarantee removal of tail-call frames, so stack space is Θ(n), even with accumulator parameters.

title: Missing progress is an error
topic: Recursion: local state, side effects and call trees

options.B: Compilation fails because post-decrement cannot be an argument
options.D: Child repeatedly receives2; use f(n-1) to make progress

explanation:
The value of n-- is the old n. The first child therefore receives 2, not 1. Every later child also receives 2 in its own new local variable.

None reaches the n=0 base case, so the stack eventually overflows. Passing n−1 makes each child argument smaller. This snippet should not be run without a bound.

title: Product-prefix snapshot
explanation:
The left pass writes [1,2,0]. At right index 2, output stays 0 and the suffix becomes 4. At index 1, output becomes 2×4=8.

The suffix then multiplies by the input zero and becomes 0. Index 0 has not received its suffix yet. The printed snapshot is [1,8,0] 0.

title: Partition before the final swap
explanation:
The pivot value is 30, but this snippet does not perform the final pivot swap. Only 20 satisfies the strict comparison. Swapping indices 0 and 2 gives [20,50,60,70,30], and i becomes 1.

The pivot remains at the last index. Answering with [20,30,60,70,50] would describe a later operation that is absent here.

title: Equal-key merge stability
explanation:
On equal values, the strict < test takes the right-hand record C first. The remaining left records A and B follow, giving CAB. A stable merge must retain the original order of equal records.

Changing < to <= selects the earlier left record on equality. That repair gives ABC without changing the sorted numeric values.

title: Voting count versus frequency
explanation:
The counter records uncanceled matches, not total occurrences. Through index 5, the surplus for candidate 2 falls to 0. The candidate field still contains 2 until index 6 chooses 1.

The final candidate is 1 with surplus 2. Value 1 occurs six times, so its frequency is 6 rather than 2.

title: One versus unlimited transaction state
explanation:
For one trade, buying at 1 and selling at 6 gives profit 5. For repeated trades, rises 1→5 and 3→6 give 4+3=7. These totals describe the prefix processed at the print point.

The last price 4 has not been processed. One-trade state and repeated-trade state answer different contracts.

title: Density comparator truncates

options.B: Integer division can hide unequal densities; compare safe cross products or double ratios
options.C: Object-array sort must always reverse equal keys
options.D: The input values cause division by zero

explanation:
Integer division turns both value-to-weight ratios into 2. The comparator therefore treats different densities as equal. Input order can then place the worse item first.

Comparing widened cross-products preserves the rational ordering for bounded integer values. Cast before multiplication. A floating-point comparison can also work within stated numeric limits, but truncating ratios cannot.

title: Dropping the wrong negative

options.A: Prints−8; track the largest negative (closest to zero) instead
options.D: Throws because negative divisors are illegal

explanation:
The nonzero product is 24. Dividing by -3 gives -8, which the faulty choice returns. The smaller product is -12 from factors -3 and 4.

To obtain it, remove -2, the negative factor closest to zero. Removing the most negative factor loses more magnitude and gives the wrong minimum.

title: Suffix maxima tie bug

options.D: 9193; use > rather than >= in the suffix update

explanation:
The equal-digit update replaces the rightmost 9 with the earlier 9. Swapping the first 1 with that earlier occurrence gives 9193. Keeping the farther-right 9 gives 9913 instead.

Both improve the first digit, but the latter preserves a larger second digit. Update the maximum index only for a strictly larger suffix digit.

title: Half-result reuse counts
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost
explanation:
The exponent chain is 13→6→3→1→0. There are five calls, including the base call. Each nonbase call stores one returned half-power and uses it twice in multiplication.

It does not call the half problem twice. That reuse gives logarithmic call count and logarithmic recursive depth.

title: Duplicate recursion hidden by multiplication
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost
explanation:
The expression contains two separate recursive calls. Multiplication does not share their results. Each call of size n creates two calls of size n/2, so T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(1).

The resulting call tree has Θ(n) entries. A numeric result of 1 does not make those executed calls disappear.

title: Widening expression placement
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost
explanation:
In -n, Java negates an int before assigning the result to long. Negating Integer.MIN_VALUE still produces the same negative int because it overflows. The later widening preserves that wrong value.

In -(long)n, widening occurs first. Long can represent the positive magnitude 2147483648, so the subsequent negation is correct.

title: Euclid snapshot
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost
explanation:
The Euclid states are (10,7), (7,3), (3,1), and (1,0). Each update sets the new pair to the old divisor and remainder. The print point occurs after the update.

Include the last iteration that produces remainder 0. At that point, the first value is the greatest common divisor, 1.

title: Square-root boundary defect
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost

options.C: true true; use <= at the square boundary

explanation:
For 49, the divisor 7 lies exactly at the square-root boundary. For 25, divisor 5 does too. A strict d*d<n test skips those checks and misclassifies both values.

The test must include equality. For unrestricted positive int values, d<=n/d also avoids overflow in d*d.

title: Two half calls plus loop
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost

options.C: Θ(nlog n) time, Θ(log n) stack

explanation:
Each call makes two calls of half the size and runs a quadratic local loop. Thus T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n²). The root's quadratic work exceeds the sum of the smaller-level work up to a constant factor.

Time is Θ(n²). Only one child path is active at once, so recursive depth is Θ(log n).

title: String centre cannot be ignored
topic: Power, Euclid, digit checks and recurrence cost

options.A: true true; the odd centre2 is never checked

explanation:
The loop checks only distinct outer positions because it uses l<r. An odd-length string's center is never examined. A center 6 or 9 does not rotate into itself, so ignoring it can accept an invalid string.

Use l<=r with correct indices. The self-mapping center digits are 0, 1, and 8.

title: Exact lower-bound interval sequence
explanation:
The search uses a half-open interval. Its bounds change as [0,5)→[0,2)→[0,1)→[1,1). On equality, moving hi to mid keeps earlier possible occurrences.

The empty final interval has boundary index 1. Moving lo on equality would instead discard the first matching position and answer a different boundary question.

title: Closed-loop no progress
explanation:
The midpoint remains 0 in the faulty closed interval. Assigning lo=mid therefore leaves lo unchanged. The same comparison repeats and the search makes no progress.

The explicit iteration cap makes this example terminate safely. For a closed interval that discards mid, use lo=mid+1. Bounds must become smaller on every unsuccessful iteration.

title: Pruned sorted count entries
explanation:
The initial interval 0..12 is mixed. It splits into 0..6 and the pure-one interval 7..12. Interval 0..6 splits into pure-zero 0..3 and pure-one 4..6.

Those are five entries in total. The pure-one lengths are 6 and 3, giving nine ones. Pure ranges stop without visiting their individual cells.

title: Pruned count asymptotics

options.A: Θ(log n) time and O(log n) stack
options.B: Θ(n) time because two calls appear

explanation:
The sorted array has only one zero-to-one transition. At any recursion level, at most one interval crosses that transition and remains mixed. Its sibling is pure and returns immediately.

There are logarithmically many levels, so the entry count is O(log n). Two written child calls do not imply two continuing branches at every level.

title: Rotation search with equality
explanation:
The first equal-border comparison removes one trailing 2. The next middle value 2 exceeds the right value 1, so lo becomes 3. Then middle value 0 is below right value 1, so hi becomes 3.

The pivot is index 3. Equal borders can require one-position reductions, making the worst case linear.

title: Fixed-point duplicate counterexample

options.A: 0, correct logarithmic search for all sorted arrays
options.B: 4, because last index equals its value
options.C: −1 despite index0 being fixed; duplicate values invalidate this half-discard rule

explanation:
The tested middle indices are 2, 3, and 4. Each middle value is below its index, so the faulty search discards the left side. That can discard a fixed point when duplicates exist.

With distinct sorted integers, a[i]−i never decreases. Duplicates remove that property, so the same half-discard proof no longer applies.

title: Row occurrence masquerades as row membership

options.B: true incorrectly; increment each value only once per row
options.C: true correctly;2 is in both rows
options.D: Change HashMap to TreeMap and counting becomes correct

explanation:
The count of 2 comes from two positions in the first row. It does not prove presence in two different rows. Count a value at most once per row, using a per-row set or a last-row marker.

Sorting or ordering the count map changes presentation only. It cannot repair the meaning of the stored count.

title: Search state after second test
explanation:
The first candidate speed 6 fits, so hi becomes 6. The second candidate speed 3 needs 10 hours, so lo becomes 4. The requested state is after that second bounds update.

Evaluate the separate ceiling for each pile before comparing hours with the limit. The bounds are not the candidate speed itself.

title: Overflow before long assignment
explanation:
The addition occurs as int arithmetic before its result reaches long. The sum wraps to a negative value. Dividing that small negative magnitude by two billion truncates to 0.

A long destination cannot undo earlier overflow. Widen one operand before the addition, so the entire ceiling numerator uses long arithmetic.

title: Ceiling is per pile
explanation:
Koko cannot spend leftover time from one pile on another pile in the same hour. Therefore, each pile needs its own rounded-up hours. The individual costs are 2,1,2,1,1, totaling 7.

Rounding the combined weight 88 divided by 22 gives 4, but that combines piles and violates the task's operation rule.

title: Predicate cost hidden inside loop

options.B: O(n log M), O(1) auxiliary space
options.C: O(n log n) due to mandatory sorting

explanation:
Each candidate-speed check scans n piles. Binary search tests logarithmically many speeds up to the maximum pile value. Multiplying those costs gives O(n log M), where M is the maximum pile.

The input piles do not need sorting. Counting only the outer search iterations incorrectly treats a full pile scan as free.

title: Contiguous partition feasibility
explanation:
With cap 17, greedy groups are [7,2,5], [10], and [8], so three groups are required. With cap 18, the groups are [7,2,5] and [10,8], so two suffice. Nonnegative values make filling each group as far as possible safe.

Negative values could change whether extending a group exceeds its final sum.

title: Cuts are counts
explanation:
LeftSize=3 and the chosen A cut imply B cut j=2. The left B border is 4, while the right A border is 2. Thus the left side contains a value larger than a right-side value.

Moving the A cut right includes more A values on the left and reduces B's left count, repairing that cross-order violation.

title: Repaired even cut
explanation:
The repaired cut puts both A values and three B values on the left. There are six total values, so the median uses the two central borders. They are 3 and 4.

Their average is (3+4)/2.0=3.5. An odd-total maximum-left rule would omit the second central value and answer incorrectly.

title: Sentinel zero is not infinity

options.A: Median is undefined whenever either array empty
options.B: Zero sentinels exclude valid negative values; use negative/positive infinity boundaries
options.D: Only the j value is wrong

explanation:
An empty left border needs a value below every permitted integer. An empty right border needs a value above every permitted integer. Zero satisfies neither condition for arbitrary signed input.

For example, it is above -1 and below positive values. Use conceptual infinities or carefully chosen safe sentinels that respect the actual input range.

title: Overflow in mean
explanation:
Java evaluates x+y as int before division. The two large values make that sum wrap to -2. Dividing afterward does not restore the correct mean.

Cast an operand to long before addition, then divide by 2.0. Casting the already evaluated sum preserves its incorrect wrapped value.

title: Incremental merge observation
explanation:
The merge selects values 1, then 2, then 3. At the snapshot, A has supplied one element and B has supplied two. The previous selected value is 2 and the current value is 3.

The total length is five, so the median is the current third value, 3, rather than the average of those two fields.

title: Set state leaked across columns
explanation:
The set still contains a from column 0. Column 1 adds b, producing two distinct stored letters even though every string agrees on b in that column. The set represents several columns instead of the current column.

Clear it before each column check. Otherwise, old state creates a false mismatch.

title: Prefix search check count
explanation:
The upper-middle candidates are prefix lengths 2, 3, and 4. All three checks succeed and each examines all three strings. These strings share gene, a four-character prefix.

The length-3 result gen would stop too early. Count actual calls to the check routine separately from the character comparisons inside each call.

title: Length search character complexity

options.A: Θ(N L log L) for N>=1,L growing
options.B: Θ(N log L) because startsWith is constant-time
options.D: Θ(NL) because binary search eliminates copying

explanation:
A prefix-length check is not constant-time. startsWith compares characters, and substring can copy them. On this worst-case input, tested lengths remain a substantial fraction of L across Θ(log L) tests.

With N strings, this can cost Θ(NL log L) character work. A direct column scan instead has a Θ(NL) worst-case bound.

title: Recursive substring cost

options.C: Θ(nlog n) time, Θ(log n) stack
options.D: Θ(n²) time and potentially Θ(n²) live characters across frames

explanation:
Recursive calls retain copied suffixes of lengths n−1, n−2, and so on. Their total retained character storage is quadratic in n. Returned-string concatenation also copies characters repeatedly.

The call stack alone is only linear, but it is not the full storage cost. Passing indices into one character array avoids those suffix copies.

title: After two finalized vertices
explanation:
After finalizing source 2, distances are [5,12,0,∞,∞]. Finalizing vertex 0 improves vertex 1 to 5+6=11 and vertex 4 to 5+13=18. Vertex 3 has no discovered path yet.

The printed state follows those two finalizations. Here, 999 stands for infinity only because the example's finite distances remain smaller.

title: Finished distance array
explanation:
Vertex 1 is reached with distance 11. Its edge to vertex 3 gives distance 11+9=20. Its edge to vertex 4 gives 11+5=16, improving the earlier 18.

Dijkstra adds an edge weight to the source-to-current distance. Copying the raw edge weight would measure a different quantity.

title: Matrix complexity despite sparse edges
explanation:
For each of V finalizations, the matrix implementation scans V candidate vertices and V possible neighbors. Even absent edges occupy scan positions. Therefore, time is Θ(V²).

Distance and visited arrays use Θ(V) extra space. The existing V×V matrix is input storage and is excluded from the question's auxiliary-space count.

title: Incorrect update behaves like Prim
explanation:
The faulty assignment stores raw edge weight 6 for vertex 1. The path through vertex 0 actually has total length 5+6=11. A shortest-path distance must include the earlier source distance.

Prim's crossing-edge key stores only an edge weight, but Dijkstra's distance does not. Using Prim's update rule changes the problem being solved.

title: Infinity addition overflow

options.C: −2147483641; guard unreachable distance before adding and use safe arithmetic
options.D: Compilation error because infinity cannot be int

explanation:
Integer.MAX_VALUE+8 wraps into a negative int. The code can then mistake an unreachable route for a very short route. Check that the current vertex is reachable before addition.

Use long distances and a safe infinity value. Merely choosing a large sentinel does not make unchecked arithmetic safe.

title: Stale heap record snapshot
explanation:
The priority queue contains both old and improved records for vertex 1. Removing the old distance-10 record does not mean expanding vertex 1 again. The stale-distance check rejects it because a better distance is already stored.

Count queue removals and useful expansions separately. They are different events in a lazy-heap implementation.

title: Negative-edge finalized vertex

options.D: No negative cycle means this must be correct

explanation:
Vertex 1 is finalized at distance 2 before vertex 2's negative edge can improve it. A path through vertex 2 later gives distance 1, contradicting the finalized value. This graph need not contain a negative cycle.

A single negative edge can invalidate Dijkstra's proof that the smallest pending distance is final.

title: Key-parent arrays halfway
topic: Prim, graph representation and MST cost
explanation:
After processing vertex 0, keys for vertices 1 and 2 are 2 and 3. Selecting vertex 1 changes vertex 2's key to crossing-edge weight 2. It also discovers vertex 3 with key 7.

Parent fields identify the selected crossing edges. These keys are edge costs for Prim, rather than accumulated distances from a source.

title: Parent replacement by crossing edge
topic: Prim, graph representation and MST cost
explanation:
The edge from vertex 2 to vertex 3 has weight 4. It improves the earlier candidate edge from vertex 1 with weight 7. Set vertex 3's key to 4 and its parent to 2.

Prim compares edges crossing from the built tree. Adding the cost of the earlier route to vertex 2 would implement a different quantity.

title: Disconnected invalid index
topic: Prim, graph representation and MST cost

options.C: −1, then prints0 because Java wraps indexes

explanation:
In the disconnected remainder, no vertex has a finite candidate key. The selection index stays -1. Reading arrays at that index throws an exception.

Check u<0 before any access. Then report disconnection, or explicitly restart to compute a forest. A restarted forest must not be presented as one spanning tree of the full graph.

title: Matrix/list scans counted
topic: Prim, graph representation and MST cost
explanation:
A matrix scan tests every possible neighbor slot, including absent edges. An adjacency list scans only stored neighbors. Their full traversal costs therefore differ even for the same sparse graph.

A constant-time matrix check for one specified pair is a separate operation. Do not use that pair-lookup cost as the cost of scanning all neighbors.

title: Zero weight is dropped
topic: Prim, graph representation and MST cost

options.A: Zero-weight edges invalidate both MST and Dijkstra
options.C: Only changing loop order repairs it
options.D: Printed degree1 omits a valid edge; existence needs its own representation

explanation:
The code treats weight 0 as an absent edge. A real zero-weight edge therefore fails the presence test and is never processed. Dijkstra and Prim can both allow zero-weight edges under their other assumptions.

Use a separate presence flag or a distinct absence sentinel. The representation must distinguish absence from a permitted weight.

title: Union does not eagerly flatten all children
explanation:
find(2) compresses the path from 2 to its current root. find(4) occurs before root 3 is attached under root 0, so 4 still points to 3 afterward. Union does not immediately visit every descendant.

Combining equal-rank roots raises root 0's rank to 2. A later find can compress the remaining 4→3→0 path.

title: Later find performs deferred compression
explanation:
Union first finds roots through 2→0 and 4→3, then attaches root 3 to root 0. The later find(4) follows 4→3→0 and replaces 4's parent with 0. Rank remains a merge heuristic.

Compression can reduce actual height without decreasing the stored rank, so rank need not equal the current measured tree height.

title: Raw child linking splits a component
explanation:
The faulty operation redirects internal node 1 rather than the root of its component. Node 1 and its descendant 2 leave node 0 behind. This splits a previously connected component in the stored structure.

A union operation must link representatives found by find. Linking arbitrary child nodes does not correctly combine whole sets.

title: Same-root rank inflation
explanation:
find(1) and find(2) both return root 0. The two values already belong to the same component. The same-root check must return without changing rank or parents.

Incrementing rank on every union call invents growth when no merge occurs. Increase rank only when two distinct equal-rank roots actually merge.

title: Parent check misses indirect root
explanation:
The parent entries are p[1]=0 and p[2]=1. They differ, but both chains lead to root 0. Comparing immediate parents therefore misses existing connectivity.

Kruskal must compare find(u) and find(v). Equal roots mean accepting the edge would close a cycle, even when the immediate parent fields differ.

title: Naive union-chain complexity
explanation:
The naive structure contains a seven-link chain from node 0 to its root. Every find(0) walks all seven links because the code does not compress paths. Eight repeated finds therefore traverse 56 links.

Union-by-rank and path-compression performance bounds require those operations to exist in the implementation. They cannot be assigned to this naive code.

title: Rejected edge still consumes index

options.C: Only final line4 3 7; continue skips the third-edge print

explanation:
The third examined edge, 0–2, is rejected because its endpoints already share a component. The continue statement skips the later print in that iteration. The next edge is accepted, giving three accepted edges and total weight 7.

Distinguish examined edges from accepted edges. Also distinguish a conceptual state from output that the control flow actually prints.

title: Disconnected guard missing

options.D: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; also require i<edges.length and check final count

explanation:
The three available edges cover a triangle on only three vertices. Two are accepted, and the third closes a cycle. The required full-tree count has not been reached, but the edge array is exhausted.

The next read goes out of bounds. Guard both the accepted-edge target and the available-edge index, then report the disconnected graph.

title: Stopping by reads is wrong
explanation:
The loop stops after reading V−1 edges. Some read edges may be rejected as cycles, so the accepted count can still be too small. Continue until V−1 edges have been accepted or no edges remain.

The index measures examined edges. The tree count measures accepted edges. Replacing one with the other changes the stopping condition.

title: Comparator overflow reverses two edges

options.D: Compilation fails because comparator cannot return int

explanation:
Subtracting opposite-extreme int weights overflows and reverses the comparator sign. The two-edge sort can therefore put the larger edge first. Use Integer.compare(a.weight,b.weight).

It compares values without an overflowing subtraction. This small example demonstrates the ordering defect directly; it does not depend on a complicated sort failure or comparator cycle.

title: Forest cost versus MST existence

options.A: 2 5 false; a minimum spanning forest, not a full spanning tree
options.B: 2 5 true; any cheapest edges form MST

explanation:
Each disconnected component can contribute its own spanning tree edge. Their total is a minimum spanning forest cost. A tree spanning all four vertices would require three accepted edges and full connectivity.

Two accepted edges cannot connect all four vertices here. The reported finite cost therefore does not prove that a full-graph MST exists.

title: Queue after a specific dequeue
topic: BFS: queue snapshots and duplicate discovery
explanation:
After removing vertex 0, the queue is [1,2]. Removing vertex 1 leaves [2], then its newly discovered neighbors 3 and 4 enter at the back. The queue becomes [2,3,4].

Marking on discovery prevents another pending route from enqueueing the same node again. Queue order follows arrival order, not numeric sorting.

title: Delayed marking duplicates work
topic: BFS: queue snapshots and duplicate discovery
explanation:
Vertices 1 and 2 both discover vertex 3 while it is still pending and unmarked. Each enqueues another copy. A queue does not automatically remove equal entries.

Mark vertex 3 when first enqueueing it, so the second discovery fails the visited test. Marking only after removal permits these duplicate pending records.

title: LIFO disguised as queue
topic: BFS: queue snapshots and duplicate discovery
explanation:
push inserts at the deque front, and pop removes from that same front. Therefore, the last pushed neighbor is removed first. Neighbor 2 is explored before neighbor 1 in this example.

That is stack order. For BFS, append at the back and remove from the front, such as addLast with removeFirst.

title: Distance set on discovery
topic: BFS: queue snapshots and duplicate discovery
explanation:
Vertex 4 is first discovered from vertex 2 at depth 2. BFS processes all earlier distance layers before later layers. In a unit-edge graph, this first discovery gives the smallest number of edges from the source.

A later route through vertex 3 cannot reduce that distance. The statement concerns edge count, rather than arbitrary weighted path cost.

title: ArrayList as queue complexity
topic: BFS: queue snapshots and duplicate discovery

options.A: Θ(n) because remove is always constant-time
options.C: Θ(1) auxiliary work including all shifts
options.D: Θ(n²), although the loop removes n items

explanation:
ArrayList.remove(0) shifts every remaining element one position. Repeating it on a queue of length n performs (n−1)+(n−2)+…+1 shifts, which is quadratic. ArrayDeque removal from the front avoids those element shifts.

Choosing a collection changes the operation cost even when the visible queue sequence is identical.

title: Mark-on-push stack order
topic: DFS ordering and the actual maze
explanation:
After processing 0, vertex 2 is already marked and waiting under vertex 1. Vertex 1 cannot recursively descend into that marked vertex 2. It instead pushes vertex 3, which is visited first.

Reversing push order alone does not reproduce recursive DFS in every graph. The point where nodes become visited also affects the traversal order.

title: Maze recursion entry trace
topic: DFS ordering and the actual maze
explanation:
The entries are (0,0), blocked (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), blocked (2,1), (1,2), and successful (2,2). Failed entries still count as calls. The successful right-hand route returns true.

Short-circuit OR then skips further alternatives. This maze makes ordinary right/down moves; it does not roll until a wall.

title: Unsafe left operand accesses first
topic: DFS ordering and the actual maze
explanation:
Java evaluates the left operand before the right operand. If g[r][c] appears before the bounds test, an invalid index throws before the guard can help. Check row and column ranges first with short-circuit operators.

Only then access the cell. Moves that can go up or left also require nonnegative-index guards.

title: Exponential no-path recursion
topic: DFS ordering and the actual maze

options.A: Always Θ(RC) because each coordinate appears once
options.C: Θ(R+C) because path depth is linear
options.D: Exponential repeated-route work despite no cycles

explanation:
Many distinct right/down routes enter the same coordinate again. Because the destination is blocked, no successful branch triggers an early return. The search explores a branching number of routes despite a linear maximum route length.

Time can be exponential while active stack depth remains linear. Caching failed states avoids repeated reachability work under fixed transitions.

title: Global seen for reachability
topic: DFS ordering and the actual maze
explanation:
The eight open cells are expanded once each after global visitation is added. The blocked destination never expands. This is valid for reachability because revisiting a cell cannot change its available future moves.

A gold-path search has a different contract: path-used cells affect future choices. Its marks must be restored rather than kept globally.

title: Second analysis consumes no land
topic: Grid islands: visitation, shape and ownership
explanation:
The first analysis changes every visited land cell to 0. The second call receives that already changed grid. It initializes a new maximum of 0 and finds no remaining land, so it returns 0.

Separate method-local totals do not restore mutated input. Use a deep copy if two independent analyses need the original grid.

title: Shallow clone still aliases rows
topic: Grid islands: visitation, shape and ownership

options.A: 0 true; cloning outer array shares its row arrays
options.B: 1 false; clone deeply copies every row

explanation:
Cloning a two-dimensional Java array copies only the outer array. Its row references still point to the original row arrays. Changing copy[r][c] therefore changes the corresponding original cell.

Clone each row to obtain independent cell storage. A new outer identity alone does not prove a deep copy.

title: Mark on enqueue exact count
topic: Grid islands: visitation, shape and ownership
explanation:
Each land cell becomes visited before it enters the queue. Later neighbors see that mark and do not enqueue it again. The area count is therefore the number of distinct discovered land cells.

Failed neighbor checks do not add area. Count discoveries separately from the number of directions tested around each cell.

title: Coordinate shape normalization
topic: Grid islands: visitation, shape and ownership
explanation:
Subtract the anchor row from each row and the anchor column from each column. These relative pairs remove position while preserving shape. Delimit both coordinates clearly and use a consistent ordering.

Translating an island then leaves the same key. Equal area alone would lose the layout information needed for shape comparison.

title: Shape keys need structural equality
topic: Grid islands: visitation, shape and ownership

options.B: 2 1; arrays use identity equality rather than element equality

explanation:

title: Short-circuit stops the second mirror pair

Map.put replaces the existing sum at the same depth. When the right subtree visits another node at that depth, its value overwrites the earlier left value. The map therefore holds the last visited value, not a level total.

The resulting means are 1, 2.5, and 5.5. BFS is one convenient grouping method, but it is not required for correct depth-based aggregation.

title: All phases on a branching tree
topic: Boundary traversal: fallbacks and duplicate leaves
explanation:
The boundary order is root, nonleaf left side, all leaves from left to right, then reversed nonleaf right side. Nodes 5 and 6 are leaves in this example. The leaf phase includes them once; side phases must exclude them.

Excluding leaves from the side phases prevents duplicates despite these fallback choices.

Adding the root unconditionally and later adding all leaves would duplicate it. A special case or mutually exclusive phases must preserve one occurrence.

Reading the input in O(n) time is a separate cost. A compact expression can describe an exponentially large result list.

Binary 011 XOR 010 becomes 001 because XOR flips the selected bit. OR with 010 leaves 011 unchanged because that bit was already set. AND with the complemented mask clears the selected bit.

Choose the operation by the required state change. Toggle, set, and clear are three different bit operations.

Java masks an int shift count to its lowest five bits. A shift by 32 therefore acts like a shift by 0 for an int. A long shift uses the lowest six bits.

Use a long literal when long-width arithmetic is required, and keep the shift count within the intended representable range.

The search tries both distinct-bike assignments. One costs 1+4=5, and the other costs 2+1=3. Every bike mark is restored after its recursive branch, so the second assignment remains available.

The returned minimum is 3. The objective is the sum for all workers, not the nearest choice for one worker.

Worker 0's nearest bike costs 1, but leaves a cost of 4 for worker 1. That total is 5. Giving worker 0 the other bike costs 2 and lets worker 1 use distance 1, totaling 3.

The local nearest assignment therefore fails. The remaining workers' costs must influence the choice.

Thus a partial cost already at least best cannot lead to a smaller total. This pruning is valid for minimum cost, but may skip equal-cost witnesses.

options.B: Same worker index makes future costs identical

The question assumes nonempty fields; an empty string would need a separate guard before reading its first character.

The no-reuse condition is separate from this divisibility condition.

Java split with default limit 0 discards trailing empty fields. A negative limit keeps them. Empty fields between separators remain a different case and are not removed by that trailing-field rule.

Pick the limit required by the input format. A line ending with a separator may intentionally contain a final empty field.

title: Dot is a regex metacharacter

The pattern dot matches any character in a Java regular expression. Splitting on it cuts at every character, and the remaining trailing empty pieces are discarded. To split on literal periods, escape the dot in the regex and escape the backslash in the Java string.

Pattern.quote is another way to treat a separator literally.
