options.B: true true; use equals/unboxing, not a general == assumption
options.D: true true; therefore == is always numeric for two wrappers

explanation:
Java guarantees sharing for boxed constant values in its small required cache range. That guarantee does not apply to arbitrary Integer values. Reference comparison with == can therefore differ from value comparison with equals.

Use equals for the stored numeric value. Do not infer a universal identity rule from one cached example or one runtime's optional cache behavior.

title: One zero versus two
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For product-except-self without division, what is the output for `[2,0,4,0]`?
explanation:
There are two zeros in the input. Excluding any one position still leaves at least one zero among the multiplied values. Every answer is therefore zero.

Prefix and suffix products handle this case without division. A special rule for exactly one zero cannot be reused for two zeros.

title: Prefix observation
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Pseudocode: `p=1; for i=0..3: ans[i]=p; p*=a[i]`, with a=[2, 3, 4, 5]. What is ans before the suffix pass?
explanation:
Start prefix at 1. Write it before multiplying the current input value. For [2,3,4,5], the successive stored values are 1,2,6,24.

Each excludes its own current value and includes only earlier factors. The later right-to-left pass supplies the missing factors to the right.

title: Space accounting
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A Θ(n) product-except-self algorithm stores prefixes in the returned n-element vector and uses two scalar accumulators. Ignoring output storage, what is auxiliary space?
explanation:
The question explicitly excludes the required output array. The working state consists of indices and two running products, so auxiliary space is Θ(1). The output itself still occupies Θ(n) positions.

Allocating separate prefix or suffix arrays would change the extra-space answer to Θ(n).

title: A bound is not a case name
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A worst-case runtime is T(n)=3n+7. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It is both O(n) and Ω(n), hence Θ(n)
options.B: Ω(n) describes only its best case
options.C: O(n²) is false because it is not tight

explanation:
The specified runtime grows linearly, so it has both upper bound O(n) and lower bound Ω(n). Matching bounds give Θ(n). It also satisfies the loose upper bound O(n²).

These symbols describe bounds on the chosen runtime function. Ω does not switch the analysis from a worst case to a best case.

title: Output dominates
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A program returns every permutation of n distinct characters as independent length-n strings. Even if recursion bookkeeping were free, what materialized-output lower bound applies?

options.A: Ω(n!) only, including all character writes

explanation:
There are n! distinct permutations of n distinct characters. Independently writing each length-n string needs n character writes.

The required output alone therefore gives Ω(n·n!) work. Returning references to shared objects is a different output representation and cannot be substituted for independently materialized strings.

title: Repeated letters
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** How many distinct complete strings can be formed by permuting `AABC`?
explanation:
Treating all four positions as distinct gives 4!=24 index permutations. The two A positions can exchange without changing the visible string. Every distinct string is counted twice, so divide by 2!=2.

There are 12 distinct strings. Repeated characters reduce value-distinct results, not the number of index orderings.

title: Unwinding output
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** C++17: `void f(int n){if(n==0)return; f(n-1); cout<<n;}`. What is printed by f(3)?
explanation:
Each call first finishes its smaller child. The base case prints nothing. On return, the suspended calls print 1, then 2, then 3, producing 123.

The increasing output order comes from printing after recursion. The active chain still has linear depth.

title: Both sides of the call
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** C++17: `void f(int n){if(n==0)return; cout<<n; f(n-1); cout<<n;}`. What is printed by f(3)?
explanation:
The entry-side prints are 3,2,1. The base call contributes no text. Returning through the calls produces the exit-side prints 1,2,3.

Combining the two phases gives 321123. Trace each print at its position before or after the child call.

title: Post-decrement fails progress
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java, deliberately faulty: `static int f(int n){if(n==0)return 0;return f(n--);}`. What happens for f(2)?
explanation:
Post-decrement evaluates to the old parameter value. Every child therefore receives 2, even though the suspended parent's local parameter later becomes 1. No child reaches zero.

Calls continue until StackOverflowError. Passing n−1 gives the child a genuinely smaller argument.

title: Fibonacci call counter
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Pseudocode: `fib(n): calls++; if n<=1 return n; return fib(n-1)+fib(n-2)`. Starting calls=0, how many invocations for fib(5), including bases?
explanation:
Count the entry itself in every call. The base counts are C(0)=C(1)=1. Then C(2)=3, C(3)=5, C(4)=9, and C(5)=15 using C(n)=1+C(n−1)+C(n−2).

The sequence value F(5)=5 is different from its invocation count 15.

title: Time versus active stack
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For unmemoized fib(n)=fib(n−1)+fib(n−2), n≥2, which pair describes time and stack?

options.A: Exponential time and exponential simultaneous stack
options.C: Θ(n) time and Θ(log n) stack

explanation:
Naive Fibonacci repeats two smaller problems and makes exponentially many total calls. Those branches execute sequentially. Only one root-to-leaf chain is active at any moment, and that chain has Θ(n) depth.

Exponential total work therefore coexists with linear call-stack space.

title: State recursion
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java: `f(n,a,b){if(n==0)return a;return f(n-1,b,a+b);}` with arbitrary-size arithmetic ignored. For f(n, 0, 1), what is guaranteed?

options.A: Θ(n) time and Θ(n) call-stack space
options.B: Θ(n) time and guaranteed Θ(1) stack

explanation:
Each call decreases n by one and performs constant local work. The full chain gives Θ(n) time. Java does not guarantee tail-call elimination, so the active frames also occupy Θ(n) space.

Accumulator parameters reduce stored sequence state but do not automatically remove recursive frames.

title: Ways at zero
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Counting ordered jumps of length 1 or2: ways(n)=ways(n−1)+ways(n−2), ways(0)=1, ways(n<0)=0. What is ways(4)?
explanation:
The five ordered step sequences are 1111,112,121,211,22. Therefore, four steps have five paths. ways(0)=1 represents the one empty continuation and gives the correct recurrence base.

Counting zero ways at zero would incorrectly remove paths that finish exactly there.

title: Generalized jumps
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Ordered jumps1..3 with ways(0)=1 and ways(n<0)=0. What is ways(4)?
explanation:
With allowed moves 1,2,3, the earlier counts are ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2, and ways(3)=4. The final move into step 4 can come from any of those positions. Thus ways(4)=4+2+1=7.

These are ordered paths, rather than unordered coin combinations.

title: Discarded immutable result
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java: `String s="abc"; s.concat("d"); System.out.print(s);` What prints?
explanation:
String.concat returns a new String. The existing string remains abc because String objects are immutable. The code discards the returned object instead of assigning it.

Calling a method that creates new text does not automatically change the variable or its original object.

title: Shared builder
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java: `StringBuilder a=new StringBuilder("ab"); StringBuilder b=a; b.append("c"); System.out.print(a);` What prints?
explanation:
Both variables refer to the same StringBuilder. Appending through either reference changes that shared object's contents, so both observe abc. Assigning one variable to a newly created builder would instead change only that reference.

Shared-object mutation and local reference reassignment have different effects.

title: Reversal recursion space
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** An in-place char-array reversal recursively swaps endpoints then calls reverse(lo+1,hi−1). For length n, absent guaranteed tail-call optimization, what is auxiliary space?
explanation:
The recursive reversal swaps opposite characters and moves inward. It therefore creates about n/2 nested calls. The array itself is reused, but each unfinished call still needs a frame.

Stack space is Θ(n). An iterative two-pointer version can perform the same swaps with constant extra space.

title: Happy-number cycle
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Repeatedly replace a positive integer by the sum of squared decimal digits. Why is “return false after10 steps” not a correctness criterion?

options.B: The map must store all integers ever existing
options.C: An arbitrary cap lacks a proof; use repeated-state detection or a proven cycle test

explanation:
Digit-square sums do not decrease on every step. An arbitrary step limit can stop without establishing either outcome. Reaching 1 proves happiness.

Repeating a non-1 state proves a cycle that will never reach 1. Use a visited-state set or a correct slow/fast cycle test.

title: Signed division
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Which pair is produced by Java `-3/2` and Python `-3//2`, respectively?
explanation:
Java integer division truncates toward zero, and its remainder retains the dividend's sign. For the stated negative operands, the pair is (-1,-2). Python floor division rounds down instead.

Applying Python's rule to a Java expression changes the quotient and remainder.

title: Hidden copying
prompt: **Extension.** Python extension: a recurrence makes two recursive calls on copied halves `a[:mid]` and `a[mid:]`, with no other work. What recurrence counts copying at each non-base call?
explanation:
Creating both half slices copies a total of Θ(n) elements in each call. The two child calls still have size n/2. The recurrence is therefore T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n).

Passing index ranges avoids this copying work, but the actual shown slicing implementation must include it.

title: Exact partition state
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Last-pivot Lomuto, strict `<`, i=lo; swap passing elements into i then swap a[i],a[hi]. After one partition of [60, 50, 20, 70, 30], which result is correct?
explanation:
Only 20 is strictly smaller than pivot 30. The scan first swaps 20 into index 0. The final swap then places 30 at index 1, giving [20,30,60,70,50].

The pivot is final, but the right interval [60,70,50] is still unsorted.

title: Duplicates and strict comparison
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Same partition on [5, 5, 5, 5] with lo0,hi3. Where is the pivot placed?
explanation:
No equal value satisfies the strict < pivot test. The smaller-region index remains 0, so the pivot is placed at index 0. All remaining equal values fall on the right.

Repeating this split creates one large recursive interval instead of balanced halves.

title: Comparison changed
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Change Lomuto condition to `a[j]<=pivot`, keeping all other rules. On [5, 5, 5, 5], pivot index?
explanation:
With <=, every scanned value equal to the pivot advances the smaller-region index. On this four-value example, the pivot finishes at index 3. The all-equal degeneration now occurs on the other side.

Changing the equality comparison alone does not create balanced partitions.

title: Nonshrinking interval
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Faulty quicksort: after last-pivot partition p, recurse `[lo,p]` and `[p+1,hi]`. Which input can make a branch retain the entire original range?
explanation:
On [1,2,3,4] with last pivot 4, partition returns the upper endpoint. Recursing on [lo,p] then repeats the whole original interval. It never shrinks.

For Lomuto, recurse on [lo,p−1] and [p+1,hi]. The pivot's final position must be excluded.

title: Linear stack despite in-place
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Strict last-pivot quicksort runs on an already sorted array of n distinct values. Time and maximum recursive depth?
explanation:
The strict last-pivot partitions repeatedly have sizes n−1 and 0 on the stated input. The work sums n+(n−1)+…+1, giving Θ(n²) time. The recursive chain has Θ(n) depth.

In-place swaps avoid an extra array, but they do not eliminate that call stack.

title: Randomization guarantee
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** After choosing pivots uniformly at random, which statement is valid for quicksort on distinct keys?

options.C: Expected Θ(nlogn), but a Θ(n²) worst case remains

explanation:
Random pivot choices give expected O(n log n) time over the random choices. An execution can still choose extremely unbalanced pivots repeatedly and take O(n²). The usual swaps also do not preserve equal-record order.

Expected performance is neither a worst-case guarantee nor a stability guarantee.

title: Strict majority
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For n=6, which minimum frequency satisfies the majority definition?
explanation:
A strict majority occurs more than n/2 times. Exactly n/2 occurrences are insufficient because another value can occupy the other half. Under that tie, no strict majority exists.

Read the strict inequality rather than replacing it with at least half.

title: Vote counter is not frequency
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Voting sets candidate when count0, then +1 for match/−1 otherwise. For [1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2], what are final candidate/count?
explanation:
The array contains six occurrences of 1. Different-value cancellations leave a final surplus counter of 2. Those are different quantities: frequency counts every occurrence, while surplus counts what remains after opposing pairs cancel.

A second pass is required when the actual frequency is requested.

title: Missing promise
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Voting on [1, 2, 3, 4] returns a candidate. What is the necessary final step to support a general majority/no-majority interface?
explanation:
Without a majority promise, a surviving candidate can have too few occurrences. A middle element in sorted order can also appear without exceeding half. Count the candidate and check frequency>n/2.

Candidate selection finds a possibility; verification establishes whether the required property holds.

title: D&C complexity
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** D&C majority with index ranges: two half candidates, if unequal count both in the current interval. Worst-case time/stack?
explanation:
The divide-and-conquer majority method can do linear combining work at each of logarithmically many levels. Its worst-case recurrence gives Θ(n log n). Equal child candidates can make a particular combine cheaper.

That shortcut does not establish a better worst-case bound for all inputs.

title: Sentinel collision
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** An implementation uses return−1 to mean no majority, while inputs may contain−1. What makes its interface ambiguous?

options.A: Negative values can never have majority

explanation:
The chosen numeric sentinel is also a permitted input value. The method cannot distinguish a real answer equal to that sentinel from absence. Return a separate status with the value, or use an optional result.

A sentinel must lie outside the valid-answer domain if it is to be unambiguous.

title: Count single-half calls
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Pseudocode: p(n) counts entry; if n==0 return1; t=p(floor(n/2)); return even? t*t:t*t*x. Calls for n=13, including base?
explanation:
The recursive exponent arguments are 13,6,3,1,0. They produce five method entries. Squaring the saved half-result performs arithmetic, not another recursive invocation.

Include the n=0 base entry, but do not count repeated use of a stored value as another call.

title: Duplicated half
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For positive n, code evaluates `power(x,n/2)*power(x,n/2)` as two independent calls at every level. What time bound replaces logarithmic time?
explanation: Two separate half-power calls create recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(1), giving Θ(n) total work. Their longest active chain still halves the exponent each time and has Θ(log n) depth. Reusing one stored half-result repairs time without changing the mathematical power identity.

title: Widen before negation
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java int n=Integer.MIN_VALUE. Which conversion correctly produces its positive magnitude?
explanation:
Negating Integer.MIN_VALUE as int overflows and leaves it negative. Casting that result to long afterward preserves the wrong value. Cast n to long before negating it.

Then the positive magnitude 2147483648 fits, and negative-exponent processing can progress correctly.

title: Integer reciprocal
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** C++17: `int x=2; double y=1/x;` What is y?
explanation:
When both operands are integers, 1/x uses integer division before any conversion to double. For an integer x above 1, the quotient is 0. Use 1.0/x to request floating division.

Assigning an already truncated quotient to double does not recover the discarded fraction.

title: Negative base
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A correct single-half power implementation computes power(−2,−3). Result?
explanation:
A negative exponent means a reciprocal. An odd exponent of a negative base also gives a negative result. Apply both rules, so the specified power retains the negative sign after inversion.

This assumes floating division; an integer reciprocal would introduce a separate truncation defect.

title: Before final merge
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Conventional recursive merge sort has finished both child sorts of [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. Full array immediately before the top merge?
explanation:
Both recursive halves have already been sorted and copied back before the final merge begins. The array therefore contains [4,5,6,1,2,3] at this snapshot. It is no longer the original descending array.

Trace the requested point after child returns, rather than reusing the initial state.

title: Inclusive split lengths
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** lo=2,hi=7,mid=lo+(hi−lo)/2=4. Left and right buffer lengths?
explanation:
The left inclusive interval 2..4 contains 4−2+1=3 elements. The right interval 5..7 contains 7−5+1=3 elements, equivalently hi−mid. Inclusive endpoints require the +1 in the left length.

Confusing lengths with last indices causes buffer and copy errors.

title: Stability on ties
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Left run records [(2,A),(2,B)], right [(2,C)]. The merge chooses right whenever keys tie. Output label order?
explanation:
With a strict comparison, the merge selects the right record first on equal keys. That record originally followed the equal left record, so their order reverses. Numeric sorting remains correct, but stability fails.

Choosing the left record with <= preserves the original equal-key order.

title: Remaining run
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Merging [1, 4] and [2, 3, 5], the main two-nonempty loop ends. Which remaining item must be appended?
explanation:
The merge emits 1,2,3,4 and then exhausts the left run. Values still remain in the right run. The main comparison loop cannot continue once one side ends, so a separate drain copies those remaining right values.

Advancing both pointers for one emitted value would skip data.

title: Sorted input time
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Unoptimized merge sort always recurses and merges on sorted input of n elements. Tight time?
explanation:
This implementation has no early check that skips an already ordered merge. Sorted input therefore still triggers the same split structure and linear merge work per level. Its time remains Θ(n log n).

Best-case claims from insertion sort or a different merge-sort implementation cannot be transferred automatically.

title: Peak versus cumulative memory
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A conventional merge sort allocates merge buffers on demand and releases them when each merge finishes. Which statement can be true?

options.B: Cumulative allocations equal peak by definition
options.C: Peak O(n) live buffer space and Θ(nlogn) cumulative allocated elements

explanation:
Adding every temporary allocation across the whole execution measures cumulative allocation traffic. Peak memory counts only objects alive at the same time. This merge-sort implementation has O(n) peak buffer storage plus O(log n) frames.

The cumulative allocated amount can be larger without increasing peak space to that same total.

title: Root-dominated case
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** T(n)=3T(n/2)+Θ(n²), base constant. Tight bound?
explanation:
For T(n)=3T(n/2)+Θ(n²), each next level has 3/4 of the preceding quadratic work. The level sum is a decreasing geometric series. The root's Θ(n²) work therefore determines the total Θ(n²).

This comparison uses 3<2²=4.

title: Equal case
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** T(n)=4T(n/2)+Θ(n²). Tight bound?
explanation:
For T(n)=4T(n/2)+Θ(n²), every level contributes Θ(n²). There are Θ(log n) levels before constant-size leaves. Multiplying level cost by level count gives Θ(n² log n).

Equal child-growth and local-work exponents create the logarithmic factor.

title: Leaves dominate
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** T(n)=16T(n/4)+Θ(n). Tight bound?
explanation:
For T(n)=16T(n/4)+Θ(n), the leaf count grows as n to log₄16, which is n². That exceeds the linear local-work exponent. The lower levels dominate, giving Θ(n²).

Calculate the branching exponent rather than choosing a case from the number of children alone.

title: Different recurrence family
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** T(n)=T(n−1)+n with T(1)=1. Tight bound and applicable method?

options.C: Θ(n²), summation rather than this Master-Theorem form

explanation:
The child size is n−1, not n divided by a fixed factor above 1. Sum the local costs directly: n+(n−1)+…+1=Θ(n²). The standard fixed-ratio Master Theorem does not apply to this recurrence.

A named theorem cannot replace its required structural assumptions.

title: Level toll
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For T(n)=3T(n/2)+n², n power of2, what is total nonrecursive work at level i?
explanation:
At depth i, there are 3ⁱ subproblems, each of size n/2ⁱ. Each node's quadratic local work is proportional to (n/2ⁱ)². Multiplying gives level work n²·(3/4)ⁱ.

Both node count and node size are necessary; considering either alone gives the wrong total.

title: O does not imply tightness
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Given only T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n), constant base, which conclusion is always supported?

options.A: T(n)=O(nlogn), but Θ(nlogn) is not established from that toll alone

explanation:
An O(n) local-work statement gives only an upper bound. The actual local work could be constant, making the recurrence's total Θ(n). A tight Θ(n log n) conclusion needs a matching linear local-work lower bound at each relevant level.

Do not replace O with Θ without supporting evidence.

title: Pruned ones call count
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** count(lo,hi) counts entry, returns0 if lo>hi or a[hi]==0, returns hi−lo+1 if a[lo]==1, else sequentially calls both halves and sums. For [0, 0, 0, 1, 1], count(0, 4) entries?
explanation:
The root interval splits into 0..2, which is all zeros, and 3..4, which is all ones. Each child returns immediately from its pure-range test. The execution therefore has the root plus two child entries.

Pruning means it does not visit every individual element.

title: Two calls do not force linear
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For the pruned sorted0/1 counter above, why is worst-case time O(logn)?

options.A: It always makes exactly one recursive call
options.B: The values are Boolean so recursion is free
options.C: At most one child per level still straddles the single0/1 boundary
options.D: Every node is pruned at the root

explanation:
Only one child interval can cross the sorted zero-to-one transition. Its sibling is pure and returns in constant time. The continuing recurrence is effectively one half-size branch per level.

Written syntax containing two calls therefore does not prove linear work when one branch stops immediately.

title: Without pruning
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A count-ones method recursively splits both halves to single elements, without endpoint shortcuts. Time?
explanation:
Without the pure-range pruning, recursion reaches n individual-element leaves. A full binary split tree also has Θ(n) internal nodes. Its height is logarithmic, but its total entries are linear.

Depth describes the longest active path; it is not the sum of all executed calls.

title: Occurrence boundaries
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For [1, 2, 2, 2, 4], first index of2=1,last=3. Which formula counts occurrences?
explanation:
The inclusive range from first to last contains last−first+1 positions. The +1 counts both endpoints. If the target is absent, first and last are absence markers and must be handled before this formula.

Arithmetic on those markers does not give a meaningful occurrence count.

title: First occurrence update
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Closed-interval binary search on equality records answer=mid. Which update seeks the earliest equal index?

options.C: hi=mid while lo<=hi without another progress rule

explanation:
An equal middle value is a candidate for the first occurrence, but an earlier equal value may still lie left. Save mid and move hi to mid−1 for the closed-interval search. Setting hi=mid can leave the interval unchanged.

The bound update must preserve earlier candidates and make progress.

title: C++ call order
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** C++17: `return traceLeft()+traceRight();` Both functions print their name. What output order is guaranteed by this expression?

options.C: Neither left-first nor right-first is guaranteed

explanation:
The question's code is C++, where the shown arithmetic operands do not establish the requested call order. Explicit sequential temporary assignments make that order clear. Java evaluates operands left to right, so its corresponding trace would be defined differently.

Language-specific evaluation rules cannot be exchanged without changing the question.

title: Rotation convention
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Ascending distinct [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] becomes [4, 5, 1, 2, 3]. Right-rotation count and minimum index?
explanation:
The minimum lies at index 2, corresponding to two right rotations under the stated convention. The same array can also result from three left rotations. Rotation count needs the direction and original sorted order.

A pivot index alone does not choose a different direction convention.

title: Duplicates degrade rotation search
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** An implementation compares a[mid] with a[hi] and on equality executes hi--. Worst-case runtime with duplicates?
explanation:
When middle and boundary values are equal, the code may only remove one trailing position. An all-equal interval can therefore require Θ(n) iterations. Distinctness supports the simpler logarithmic guarantee.

Duplicates are a change in the search proof, not just another ordinary test value.

title: Fixed point fails with duplicates
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Faulty fixed-point search uses `if a[mid]<mid: lo=mid+1` on any sorted array. Which input demonstrates losing an existing fixed point?
explanation:
At middle index 2, value 0 is below its index, so the faulty method discards the left side. That side contains fixed point index 0. Duplicates allow a[i]−i to decrease, invalidating the monotone argument.

The distinct-value fixed-point search cannot be used unchanged for this array.

title: Row counting bug
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Rows [[2, 2],[3, 4]]. A hash counter increments per occurrence and declares a value common when count equals row count2. False output?
explanation:
Two occurrences in one row do not imply membership in two rows. The count map must receive one contribution per row for each value. Deduplicate the row or store the last contributing row index.

A common-element test asks which rows contain the value, rather than how many positions contain it.

title: Flattened ordering
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Rows [1, 4, 7] and [2, 5, 8] are individually sorted. Can ordinary binary search on the flattened row-major array be justified?

options.A: Yes, row sorting implies global ordering
options.B: No; the flattened sequence drops from7 to2
options.C: Yes, because all values are positive
options.D: Only when the target is absent

explanation:
Each row is sorted internally, but a later row can start below an earlier row's final value. Flattening can therefore create a decrease between rows. One global binary search requires globally sorted flattened order.

Searching each row separately uses only the weaker rowwise-sorting premise that is actually provided.

title: Exact prefix
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Longest common prefix of gene, genesis, general?
explanation:
All three strings begin with the four characters g,e,n,e. The first string then ends, so no fifth shared character is possible. The exact prefix is gene.

A summary that says gen is incorrect for these inputs. Direct character tracing can reveal an error in a prepared note.

title: Set not cleared
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For words ["ab","ab"], a set is retained across columns; after inserting each column, code requires set.size()==1. Returned prefix length?
explanation:
Column 0 leaves a in the set. Column 1 adds b without removing a, giving {a,b} despite agreement within column 1. The set then describes multiple columns instead of one.

Clear it at the start of each column. Resetting state is part of preserving the comparison's meaning.

title: Character work
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Straightforward binary search on prefix length repeatedly scans prefixes with startsWith. On N identical strings each of length L, character work can be?
explanation: Binary-searching prefix length uses Θ(log L) checks, but each check can compare Θ(L) characters per string. For N strings, the worst-case character work can be Θ(NL log L). Monotone feasibility justifies binary search; it does not make the feasibility routine constant-time.

title: Java equality
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java: `new String("ab")==new String("ab")`. What is the value?
explanation:
The two explicit String constructions create different objects. The == expression compares references and therefore reports false. equals compares their character contents and reports true.

Content equality and object identity are separate tests, even when both variables display the same text.

title: Empty member
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A vertical LCP scan first computes minimum string length. For ["abc",""], what should it return under the normal contract?
explanation:
One member has length 0, so no character position is shared by every string. The common prefix is empty. Calculate the shortest length or check length before indexing a column.

Reading charAt(0) on the empty string would throw instead of producing the required empty result.

title: Hours trace
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** At k=22, piles [30, 11, 23, 4, 20] need how many total hours?
explanation:
The separate pile-hour ceilings are 2,1,2,1,1. Their sum is 7. Taking ceil(totalBananas/speed) would combine several piles into one hour budget and violate the one-pile-per-hour operation rule.

The feasibility test must match the allowed operation, not only the aggregate quantity.

title: First feasible speed
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Same piles, h=6. Minimum feasible integer speed?
explanation:
At speed 22, the total is 7 hours. At speed 23, the pile costs are 2,1,1,1,1, totaling 6. Increasing speed cannot increase required hours.

Therefore, if the limit is 6, speed 23 is the first feasible candidate once the slower boundary has been checked.

title: Predicate direction
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Binary search minimizes speed. At mid the total hours exceed h. Which update is justified?
explanation:
Too many hours mean the candidate speed is too small. Every slower speed takes at least as many hours and also fails. Search the larger-speed interval.

Moving toward smaller speeds after an infeasible result reverses the predicate's direction and can discard every valid answer.

title: Widening too late
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java: `int p=2_000_000_000,k=2_000_000_000; long hours=(p+k-1)/k;` Why is the arithmetic faulty?

options.A: The int numerator overflows before assignment to long
options.B: Division by k is always a floating operation
options.C: The long destination prevents any overflow
options.D: p itself exceeds Java int range

explanation:
The individual pile and speed values fit int, but p+k−1 can exceed its range. Cast p to long before the addition. The widened numerator then gives the correct ceiling of 1.

Assigning the already overflowed numerator to long would retain the incorrect value.

title: Correct search cost
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** n piles, maximum M; each feasibility test scans all piles, binary search over integer speed1..M. Worst-case time?

options.B: O(nlogn) because piles must be sorted

explanation:
Binary search operates on candidate speed values, not on pile indices. Each candidate requires a full pile scan. The resulting cost is O(n log M), with M the largest pile.

Sorting the piles is unnecessary because the hour sum does not depend on their order.

title: Multiset preserves duplicates
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Median of sorted arrays [1, 2] and [2, 3]?
explanation:
The combined sorted multiset is [1,2,2,3]. Both occurrences of 2 remain because each is a separate data item. The median uses the two middle values, both 2.

Deduplicating would change the distribution to [1,2,3] and solve a different statistical problem.

title: Integer averaging trap
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java/C++ with safe small ints: `(2+3)/2` assigned to double. Value?
explanation:
The code performs integer division before converting the quotient to double. That discards any fractional half. Use a safely widened sum divided by 2.0.

The numeric type must be correct when the operation executes; changing the destination type afterward cannot recover the lost fraction.

title: Partition counts
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A length 2, B length 5; cut i=1 in A. With leftSize=(m+n+1)/2, what is B cut j?
explanation:
The desired left size is 4 and cutA is 1. Therefore, cutB=4−1=3. A cut value counts how many elements enter the left group.

It is not the index of the final left element. The relevant border element has index cut−1 when the cut is positive.

title: Direction of correction
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Partition has maxLeftA=9,minRightB=4. How should cutA move?
explanation:
The left A border is too large compared with the right B border. Reduce A's left-element count by moving its cut left. The derived B cut then moves right.

Those changes remove an excessive A value from the left and include more B values, repairing the cross-order condition.

title: Even partition result
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A=[1, 3],B=[2, 4], valid cuts i=1,j=1. Median?
explanation:
The valid cut has largest left border max(1,2)=2 and smallest right border min(3,4)=3. With even total length, the median is their average, 2.5. Widen the addition if necessary and divide by 2.0.

Reading only the largest left border would use the odd-length rule.

title: Empty-side boundaries
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A empty,B=[2, 4, 6]. Correct odd median partition result?

options.D: Always reject if either array empty

explanation:
An empty array contributes conceptual negative infinity on its left border and positive infinity on its right border. The nonempty array then supplies the actual median values. An empty member alone is valid.

Only a total length of zero lacks a median and needs rejection under this contract.

title: Smaller-array reason
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Why swap arrays so partition binary search runs on the smaller one?

options.A: It reduces search cost and keeps complementary cut within bounds for the usual full search interval
options.B: It makes the larger array unsorted

explanation:
Search cut i in the shorter array of length m≤n. The derived j=(m+n+1)/2−i then stays within 0..n. The search has m+1 cut positions, giving O(log(min(m,n)+1)) time.

The shorter-array choice supports both valid boundaries and the smaller search cost.

title: Optimal fractional value
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Items(value,weight)=(60, 10),(100, 20),(120, 30),capacity50. Fractional optimum?
explanation:
Take weight 10 for value 60 and weight 20 for value 100. Capacity 50 then has 20 units left. Take 20/30 of the last item's value 120, adding 80.

Total value is 240. Taking all three items would require weight 60 and exceed capacity.

title: Fractions tracked
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For the same instance, original-order selected fractions?
explanation:
The item densities are 6,5,4 in descending order. The first two consume weight 30, leaving 20. Fractional knapsack permits taking that 20 from the third item's weight 30.

The fractions are therefore 1,1,2/3. A 0/1 task would forbid that final fraction.

title: Raw value is insufficient
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Capacity10, fractional items(value,weight)=(100, 100),(60, 10). Raw-value descending selects the first fraction. Its value and the density-optimal value?
explanation:
One item gives value 10 for weight 10, a density of 1. The other gives value 60 for the same weight, a density of 6. Raw total value can favor a heavy low-density item on other inputs.

Fractional selection must compare value per unit weight, not only the item's displayed value.

title: Integer ratio ties
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** C++ `value/weight` computed as int gives ratios for (5, 2) and (7, 3). What information is lost?

options.A: Both truncate to2, hiding the true ordering2.5>7/3

explanation:
Integer ratio calculations can truncate distinct densities to the same number. That creates a false tie and can reverse the needed order. Floating ratios within numeric limits or safely widened cross-products preserve the ordering.

A genuine equal-density tie is harmless for value; a truncation-created tie is not.

title: Why fractional exchange works
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A solution contains weight from a lower-density item while some higher-density item remains available. With fractions allowed, exchanging equal weights does what?
explanation:
Move equal weight from a lower-density chosen fraction to a higher-density available fraction. Capacity use stays unchanged, and value does not decrease. Repeating this exchange yields density order.

Indivisible items may not permit equal-weight replacement, so this fractional proof does not automatically justify 0/1 knapsack greedy.

title: 0/1 has optimal substructure
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Which statement correctly explains failure of ratio greedy for general0/1 knapsack?

options.C: The greedy choice can fail even though the problem has optimal substructure

explanation:
A problem can have optimal substructure without supporting the proposed greedy choice. 0/1 knapsack can be decomposed into smaller optimal choices, but density-first may still discard the best whole-item combination. Fractional splitting permits exchanges that the indivisible contract forbids.

The permitted operations determine whether the local proof applies.

title: Class coin counterexample
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Unlimited coins1, 3, 4, 5, amount 7. Greedy count and true minimum count?
explanation:
Largest-first takes 5, then 1, then 1, using three coins for amount 7. The legal choice 3+4 uses two. Since two is better than three, this one input disproves general optimality of the greedy rule.

It does not imply greedy fails for every denomination system.

title: Unreachable remainder
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Descending coin greedy on [6, 4],amount 5 uses4. What must the interface acknowledge?

options.A: Leftover1, so exact change was not produced
options.B: One coin is a valid exact answer
options.C: Return0 coins because greedy is always optimal

explanation:
Without a coin of value 1, some remainders cannot be formed. A greedy pass can therefore stop with a nonzero remainder, which is not valid exact change. Check feasibility rather than reporting the coins already chosen as a complete answer.

Representability and minimum coin count are separate requirements.

title: Coin output cost
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For amountA, k denominations, compare repeated coin output with counts `(denomination,count)`.

options.B: Counts require more than A records
options.D: Counts avoid Θ(A) output when denomination1 supplies the amount

explanation:
Printing A separate one-value coins requires Θ(A) output entries. An algorithm cannot materialize that list in less than its output size. A count representation can instead use at most one record per denomination.

That changes output cost but does not prove the selected counts are optimal.

title: Activity selection trace
prompt: **Extension.** Half-open intervals [1, 3),[2, 4),[3, 5),[0, 6),[5, 7). Earliest-finish greedy selects how many?
explanation:
Select [1,3), then [3,5), then [5,7). Each next start equals the preceding finish, which is compatible under this half-open interval contract. The selected count is three.

If a task defines endpoints differently, the comparison must follow that contract rather than a memorized strictness rule.

title: Wrong greedy criterion
prompt: **Extension.** Intervals [0, 10),[1, 2),[2, 3),[3, 4). Earliest-start-first accepts0..10. Maximum compatible count?
explanation:
The three short intervals fit consecutively, while choosing the earliest-start long interval blocks them. Earliest finish has an exchange proof: it leaves at least as much room for the remaining schedule. Earliest start alone lacks that guarantee.

The example shows why the sorting key must follow the proof.

title: Neighbour scan
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A graph has V vertices and adjacency matrix. Enumerating all neighbours of a given vertex costs?
explanation:
A matrix can check one specified edge in O(1), but enumerating all neighbors still scans V slots. An adjacency list already stores just the present neighbors. Therefore, neighbor enumeration is O(V) for a matrix row and O(degree) for a list.

Lookup cost and full enumeration cost are different operations.

title: Undirected list storage
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** An ordinary adjacency list represents an undirected graph with V vertices,E edges, storing each edge at both endpoints. Space?
explanation:
An undirected adjacency list stores one list head per vertex and normally two neighbor records per edge. Storage is Θ(V+2E), which simplifies to Θ(V+E). The factor 2 does not change growth order.

A matrix instead stores V² possible-pair slots, including absent edges.

title: Zero ambiguity
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** A weighted matrix uses0 to mean no edge. What valid Dijkstra-compatible feature can it fail to represent?
explanation:
Dijkstra allows edge weight zero because its proof requires nonnegative weights. A representation using zero for absence cannot represent that legal edge. Store presence separately or choose a distinct absence sentinel.

The algorithm's weight assumption and the representation's encoding rule must both be satisfied.

title: Directed matrix
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Matrix entries w[0][1]=5,w[1][0]=0 where0 means absence. What can be inferred?

options.B: A directed edge0→1 need not have the reverse edge
options.C: A symmetric matrix is compulsory for every graph
options.D: No graph can have this matrix

explanation:
A directed edge u→v does not imply an edge v→u. Its adjacency matrix therefore need not be symmetric. An undirected representation normally stores both directions and has symmetric entries.

Check the graph's direction contract before imposing a matrix symmetry condition.

title: Relaxation arithmetic
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** dist[u]=5,weight(u,v)=6,current dist[v]=12. Correct new tentative distance?
explanation:
The current source distance is 5 and the edge weight is 6. The route through that vertex has length 11. Since 11 improves the earlier 12, relaxation stores 11.

Storing raw edge weight 6 would omit the route already traveled and confuse shortest-path distance with a crossing-edge key.

title: Next finite vertex
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Tentative distances[5, 12, 0,∞,∞], vertex2 already visited. Which unvisited vertex is chosen next?
explanation:
Vertex 0 has the smallest finite pending distance, 5, so it is selected next. The vertex label 0 is its identity, not its distance. Selection compares recorded distances of unsettled vertices.

Unreachable vertices with infinity cannot beat a finite candidate.

title: Matrix runtime
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Dijkstra selects minimum unvisited distance by scanning V entries, then scans a V-entry row, for up to V vertices. Time?
explanation:
Each outer iteration performs two separate scans of length V: one to select a vertex and one to inspect its matrix neighbors. Their sum is O(V), not O(V²) per iteration. Across V iterations, time is O(V²).

The two scans are sequential, rather than three nested V-length loops.

title: Nonnegative requirement
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Which weight restriction is sufficient for standard Dijkstra correctness?

options.B: All edges nonnegative; zero is allowed
options.C: Any weights if no negative cycle
options.D: Negative undirected edges are always fine

explanation:
Dijkstra requires nonnegative edge weights. A negative edge can produce a shorter route to a vertex that was already finalized. Weight zero is allowed because it cannot create that decrease through a farther pending route.

The representation must still distinguish a zero-weight edge from absence.

title: Counterexample with negative edge
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Directed edges s→a: 2,s→b: 5,b→a:−4. Dijkstra finalizes a before b. True shortest s→a?

options.A: 1, so finalizing2 without revisits is wrong
options.D: There must be a negative cycle

explanation:
The route s→b→a costs 1, but a was finalized earlier with a larger value. The graph has no directed cycle, so a negative cycle is not needed to cause failure. The negative edge alone invalidates Dijkstra's finalization argument.

A different shortest-path method is required for this contract.

title: Disconnected case
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** All remaining unvisited distances are∞. A matrix implementation has no finite chosen index. What should it do?

options.D: Stop/reject unreachable vertices rather than index with an invalid choice

explanation:
Vertices outside the source's component retain infinity. Once no finite pending distance remains, a selection index may stay invalid. Stop or handle that state before indexing the matrix.

Also avoid adding edge weights to infinity. Disconnection is a valid graph condition, not permission for out-of-bounds access.

title: One versus unlimited
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** prices=[7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4], no fee/cooldown. One-transaction and unlimited maximum profits?
explanation:
One trade can buy at 1 and sell at 6, earning 5. Unlimited fee-free trades can take rises 1→5 and 3→6, earning 4+3=7. Both answers use the same price array.

They differ because the permitted action sequences differ.

title: Update invariant
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** One-transaction scan has minPrice=1,best=4 before price3. After processing3, state?
explanation:
The smallest earlier price remains 1. The current possible sale profit is 2, below the previously recorded best 4. Keep best=4.

The two fields describe different facts: minimum is a candidate buy price, while best is the largest completed buy/sell gain seen so far.

title: Declining market
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** prices=[9, 7, 4, 1], at most one buy/sell and doing nothing allowed. Profit?
explanation:
Every later sale price is below the relevant earlier buy price. No profitable transaction exists. Best starts at 0 to represent choosing no trade, so the result remains 0.

Initializing from a compulsory losing transaction would change the optional-trade contract.

title: Summing rises
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Unlimited prices=[1, 2, 2, 5, 3, 4]. Sum of positive adjacent differences?
explanation:
The positive adjacent gains are 1,0,3,0,1, totaling 5. Negative moves contribute nothing. A zero change also contributes nothing.

Under unlimited trades with no fee or cooldown, each rising run's gain equals its positive adjacent differences. The formula relies on those rules.

title: Fee extension invalidates formula
prompt: **Extension.** Extension: prices=[1, 3], fee1 per completed transaction. Plain sum-positive-differences returns2. Correct net profit?
explanation:
The gain of 2 incurs fee 1, leaving profit 1. Summing the raw positive price rise would report 2 and ignore the fee. Adding a fee changes the trading contract.

The no-fee greedy formula therefore needs replacement or a new proof for any proposed modification.

title: Even negatives
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Minimum nonempty subset product of [−2,−3, 4]?
explanation:
All nonzero factors multiply to 24. With two negative factors, remove the negative closest to zero, -2. The remaining product is 24/(-2)=-12.

Removing -3 gives -8, which is larger and therefore worse for minimization. The subset may omit an input value.

title: Zeros do not force zero
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Minimum subset product of [−1, 0]?
explanation:
The subset does not have to include every value. Selecting the single -1 gives product -1, which is below zero. Zeros therefore do not force a zero answer when a negative product is available.

The nonempty-subset requirement still permits a singleton.

title: All positives
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Minimum nonempty subset product of integer values[2, 3, 5]?
explanation:
All values are positive integers and the smallest is 2. A nonempty singleton containing 2 has product 2. Multiplying several factors at least 1 cannot improve on that smallest permitted value.

An empty product of 1 is not available because the subset must be nonempty.

title: Even negative units
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Minimum nonempty subset product of [−1,−1]?
explanation:
Selecting both negative unit values gives positive product 1. Selecting only one gives -1, which is smaller. The even-negative case must allow omitting one factor.

Keeping all nonzero values is therefore not always correct for minimum subset product.

title: Integers are an assumption
prompt: **Extension.** Extension: apply “multiply all nonzeros with odd negative count” to real values[−10, 0.2]. It returns−2. True minimum nonempty subset product?
explanation:
The integer-factor assumption supports taking positive factors of magnitude at least 1. A positive real factor below 1 instead reduces a negative product's magnitude and makes it less negative. For example, multiplying -2 by 0.5 gives -1.

The class integer rule cannot be generalized to arbitrary real values unchanged.

title: Tie chooses rightmost
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** At most one swap on1993. Largest result?
explanation:
Swap the first 1 with the later 9 to obtain 9913. Using the earlier 9 gives 9193. Result 9931 would require further rearrangement beyond one swap.

Choose the rightmost equal maximum because it preserves the larger earlier suffix after the first-digit improvement.

title: Suffix maximum indexes
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** For digits84725, rightmost suffix-maximum indices for each position?
explanation:
Scanning digits from the right, value 5 at index 4 dominates the nearby 2. Value 7 at index 2 then becomes the suffix maximum for index 1. Value 8 at index 0 dominates the whole suffix.

The stored fields are positions of maximum digits, not the digits themselves.

title: Only one exchange
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Maximum Swap result for84725?
explanation:
The first improvable position contains digit 4, and its suffix contains maximum digit 7. Swap those positions and stop. Earlier fixed digits cannot improve, and this leftmost improvement outweighs changes farther right.

Sorting every digit could yield a larger arrangement, but violates the one-swap limit.

title: Equal maximum update
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Scanning suffixes right-to-left, new digit equals currently tracked maximum. To retain rightmost tie, should the index update?

options.B: No; update only on strictly larger digit

explanation:
On an equal suffix maximum, the stored occurrence is already farther right. Keep that index. A later swap then places the displaced smaller digit farther to the right, preserving earlier large digits.

Replacing the stored index on equality would choose a weaker equal-value swap.

title: Edge count
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** An undirected connected graph has6 vertices. Any spanning tree contains how many edges?
explanation:
A connected acyclic graph on V vertices has V−1 edges. Every spanning tree therefore has that edge count. Edge weights determine which spanning tree has minimum total cost, but do not change the required count.

A disconnected forest has fewer edges unless components are joined.

title: Keys differ from distances
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Prim key[u]=4,edge(u,v)=3,current key[v]=5. Correct updated key[v]?
explanation:
Prim's key is the weight of one edge crossing into the growing tree. It does not measure a route from the start. Adding key[u] to an outgoing edge therefore changes its meaning.

Dijkstra adds a source distance, while Prim compares the new edge weight alone.

title: Objective contrast
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Triangle edges0–1: 2, 1–2: 2, 0–2: 3. MST edges versus source0 shortest-path tree?

options.B: MST requires edge3 because it is direct
options.C: MST uses2+2; shortest-path tree uses edges2 and3

explanation:
The minimum spanning tree has total edge weight 4 through its chosen chain. The direct route 0→2 has path cost 3, below the chain's path cost 4. Minimizing the sum of tree edges does not minimize every source-to-vertex path.

MST and shortest-path objectives differ.

title: Negative weights in MST
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Connected undirected graph has some negative edge weights. What about MST algorithms Prim/Kruskal?

options.A: They require nonnegative edges like Dijkstra
options.B: Negative weights are allowed for the MST objective
options.C: They must reject all negative graphs
options.D: A negative edge makes spanning trees undefined

explanation:
Negative weights do not prevent an MST from existing in a connected finite graph. A spanning tree uses a finite edge subset and contains no cycle. It cannot repeatedly traverse a negative cycle to decrease its objective indefinitely.

Dijkstra's nonnegative requirement must not be imposed on MST algorithms.

title: Disconnected Prim
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Prim from vertex0 exhausts all finite keys while some vertices remain unselected. What is indicated?

options.A: Graph disconnected; no spanning tree over all vertices
options.B: An MST already spans all vertices
options.C: The key array must be reset to zero
options.D: Every remaining vertex is a leaf of the same tree

explanation:
The disconnected graph has no single tree spanning all vertices. An unguarded Prim run can fail when no finite key remains. A deliberately restarted algorithm can produce a minimum spanning forest.

State that changed output contract explicitly instead of labeling the forest as a full spanning tree.

title: Root differs from direct parent
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** parent=[0, 0, 1, 3]. find(2) follows parents recursively. Returned representative?
explanation:
Node 2 points to 1, and 1 points to 0. Its immediate parent is 1, but its component representative is 0. find follows the full parent chain.

Testing only parent[2] does not identify the root unless compression has already made that direct link.

title: Path compression write
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Same parent array, after compressed find(2), what becomes parent[2]?
explanation:
Path compression writes the found root into the parent field of each visited nonroot node. A chain 2→1→0 can become 2→0 and 1→0. The component membership does not change.

The operation improves later root lookups by shortening the paths it actually visited.

title: Attach roots only
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** parent=[0, 0, 2, 2]. To unite components containing1 and3, which conceptual action is correct?

options.A: Set parent[1]=3 only; all of component0 must move automatically
options.B: Find roots0 and2 and link one root under the other
options.C: Set parent[0]=1 to create a cycle
options.D: Change rank without changing any parent

explanation:
Reparenting an arbitrary child can detach that child's descendants from their earlier root. That can split a stored component instead of merging two complete components. Find both roots first and attach one root to the other.

Roots represent the full sets that union is intended to combine.

title: Unequal-rank union
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Roots a,b have ranks3, 1. Standard union-by-rank attaches b below a. New rank[a]?
explanation:
When ranks differ, attach the lower-rank root under the higher-rank root. The winner's rank does not need to increase. Only combining two distinct equal-rank roots triggers an increment in this rule.

Rank is a height-related merge heuristic, rather than a counter for every union call.

title: Equal ranks
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Two different roots both rank2 are united under one chosen root. New rank of chosen root?
explanation:
Two equal-rank roots can produce a tree with one extra level when one is attached beneath the other. Increase the winning root's rank by 1. The losing node is no longer a root, so its stored rank does not direct later root-level choices.

A same-root union must not increment rank.

title: Amortized is not per-call constant
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** With union by rank and path compression, standard bound for a long operation sequence?

options.A: Every individual find is worst-case O(1)
options.D: Path compression removes the need to follow parents ever

explanation:
The inverse-Ackermann bound describes amortized cost across a sequence using rank and compression. It does not mean every individual find takes exactly one step. An initial find may traverse several links before compressing them.

Distinguish an amortized growth bound from a literal constant number of operations per call.

title: Cycle test
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Accepted edges0–1 and1–2. Candidate edge0–2. DSU roots of0 and2 agree. Action?

options.A: Accept because direct parents might differ
options.B: Reject it as forming a cycle

explanation:
Equal endpoint roots mean the accepted forest already contains a path between those vertices. Adding the edge closes a cycle, so Kruskal rejects it. Different immediate parent entries do not change that conclusion.

The root comparison tests connectivity through any number of parent links.

title: Acceptance count
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** V=4, sorted edges(0, 1, 1),(1, 2, 2),(0, 2, 3),(2, 3, 4). MST total weight?
explanation:
Accept the edges of weights 1 and 2. Reject weight 3 because it closes a cycle. Accept weight 4 to join the remaining component.

The tree has three accepted edges and total 7. Four edges were examined, showing why the stopping count must track accepted edges.

title: Necessary not sufficient
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** V=4,E=3 with triangle0–1, 1–2, 2–0 and isolated3. Does E≥V−1 prove connectivity?

options.B: Only if weights positive, then yes
options.C: A triangle automatically covers all vertices

explanation:
Having at least V−1 edges is necessary for connectivity, but not sufficient. Many edges can lie inside one component while another vertex remains isolated. Check connectivity through accepted component joins.

Edge quantity alone does not establish that a spanning tree exists.

title: Exhausted list
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Kruskal loops until accepted=V−1 but never checks nextIndex<E. On a disconnected graph, likely code failure?

options.A: It correctly returns an MST every time
options.B: It must find a new edge automatically
options.D: It always terminates after exactly V−1 reads

explanation:
The edge list ends before V−1 edges are accepted. The next unguarded read goes beyond the list. Stop when edges are exhausted, then check the accepted count.

Report a forest or no full spanning tree when components remain. The loop needs both progress and exhaustion conditions.

title: Comparator overflow
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Java comparator returns `a.weight-b.weight`. For a.weight=2_000_000_000,b.weight=−2_000_000_000, what is the defect?

options.A: Both weights individually exceed int range
options.B: Subtraction overflows int and can reverse ordering
options.D: Comparison returns only0 or1 by language rule

explanation:
A subtraction comparator can overflow and reverse weight order. Kruskal's proof assumes actual ascending weights, so that defect can invalidate the result. Use Integer.compare or Long.compare for the corresponding type.

A syntactically successful sort is not evidence that an overflow-prone comparator imposed the intended order.

title: BFS order specified
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Graph adjacency in ascending order: 0:[1, 2], 1:[0, 3], 2:[0, 3], 3:[1, 2]. BFS from0 marks on enqueue. Dequeue order?
explanation:
FIFO order processes all depth-1 vertices before any depth-2 vertex. Node 3 is marked when first discovered and therefore enters the queue once. Follow the stated neighbor order within a layer.

BFS layer order is guaranteed, while a different neighbor list can change order among equal-depth nodes.

title: Marking too late
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** Same graph, visited only when dequeued and no pending-state check. What can happen before3 is dequeued?
explanation:
When vertex 2 examines vertex 3, vertex 3 is pending but still unmarked. It is therefore enqueued again. Mark on enqueue rather than only on removal to prevent duplicate pending entries.

The queue itself has no rule that deduplicates equal vertices.

title: Shortest-path condition
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** BFS first-discovery depth minimizes what in an unweighted graph?

options.C: Number of edges from the source

explanation:
Every BFS layer adds one edge to the path length. In an unweighted or unit-weight graph, first discovery therefore minimizes the number of edges. For arbitrary edge weights, fewer edges need not mean smaller total weight.

The shortest-path guarantee must match the edge-cost contract.

title: Source coverage
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** BFS starts in one component of a disconnected graph. What is needed to visit every vertex?

options.A: The first queue eventually jumps components
options.B: Start additional traversals from remaining unvisited vertices
options.C: Add all edges to a stack

explanation:
A traversal from one source reaches only that source's connected component. No edge can take it into a separate component. To cover the whole graph, start another traversal at each still-unvisited vertex.

This changes the outer coverage loop, rather than the local neighbor traversal rule.

title: FIFO versus LIFO
prompt: **Class-based scenario.** BFS-like code uses push_back and pop_back from the same sequence rather than removing the front. What changes?

options.A: It uses LIFO exploration, so BFS level-order guarantees no longer apply

explanation:

Decimal-string addition avoids overflow for fields beyond fixed-width range.

title: Factorial returns versus calls

Call count, base result, and final factorial are three different measurements and must not be substituted for one another.

The static counter retains its earlier value between top-level method invocations. The first tree contributes three calls, and the second contributes two. The total is five unless the code explicitly resets it.

title: Negative greedy transfer limits

prompt: **Extension.** Extension: split-array feasibility repeatedly extends a part until its sum would exceed limit, then cuts. Why is the standard proof based on nonnegative elements?

title: the output itself imposes a lower bound

The correct generator returns Q strings of length n by concatenating at each layer, then sorts them using comparison-based sorting. Which analysis is valid under the stated character-cost model?

title: the same multiplication differs by language

options.A: Java prints -2147479015; corresponding C++ signed multiplication overflows with undefined behaviour
